newsitem.title: USA: NFL AMERICAN FOOTBALL-PACKERS FAVORED TO RETURN TO GLORY DAYS.
newsitem.headline: NFL AMERICAN FOOTBALL-PACKERS FAVORED TO RETURN TO GLORY DAYS.

text.p: Twenty-nine years after legendary coach Vince Lombardi was carried off the field on the shoulders of his victorious Green Bay Packers, the NFL's most fabled franchise is poised to reclaim its past glory.
The Packers, a virtual dynasty in the 1960s which has longed to regain its luster, take on the youthful New England Patriots Sunday at the Louisiana Superdome in the 31st edition of the Super Bowl.
And if the formidable Packers live up to expectation, Green Bay, Wisconsin will again become "Titletown, USA," it's nickname in the days of Lombardi and company.

The Packers were pre-season favourites to win the Super Bowl after knocking on the door last year, and they maintained that status throughout a 13-3 season and impressive playoff victories over the San Francisco 49ers and Carolina Panthers.

They have been installed as whopping 14-point favourites to beat the Patriots, the latest in a long line of AFC underdogs in the big game that has seen the the NFC representative win the last 12 Super Bowls.
"This is a team that should have been in the Super Bowl last year," Green Bay's veteran defensive end Sean Jones said of his team's tough loss to Dallas in the 1996 NFC title game.
"If we don't win this game, then I think the season will be a failure," added Jones, whose opinion is shared by most of his teammates, if not laid-back head coach Mike Holmgren.
The Packers appear to be a team without an exploitable weakness.
They scored more points than any team in the National Football League this season, while allowing the fewest. No team has been rated first in both categories since the undefeated 1972 Miami Dolphins.

Their offensive success begins with brilliant quarterback Brett Favre, who was named the league's Most Valuable Player for a second successive season after leading the league with 39 touchdown passes.

And Green Bay's often overlooked running backs have come into their own in recent weeks with Edgar Bennett and Dorsey Levens emerging as post-season heroes, making the Packers almost as dangerous on the ground as in the air.
Their solid defence is anchored by defensive ends Jones and all-time sacks leader Reggie White, an ordained minister who believes God sent him to Green Bay to win a Super Bowl.
In the defensive backfield, seasoned veterans LeRoy Butler and Eugene Robinson make passing against the Pack no picnic.

Even on special teams the Packers are scary, featuring the explosive punt returning of former Heisman Trophy winner Desmond Howard, who almost single-handedly staked Green Bay to a 14-0 lead over the 49ers before they knew what hit them.
The Patriots, who went from 6-10 last year to 11-5 this season, are themselves no slouches at piling up points.

New England finished second only to Green Bay in points scored behind talented, young quarterback Drew Bledsoe, who has a trio of dangerous targets in speedy wideouts Terry Glenn and Shawn Jefferson and tight end Ben Coates.
Providing balance in the attack is the slippery Curtis Martin, who rushed for 1,152 yards this season.
But the Patriots are a very young team, prone to mistakes under pressure. And the Packers will surely supply plenty of pressure.
The main reason the Patriots cannot be taken lightly, however, is "the Parcells factor" -- the experience of coach Bill Parcells, winner of two Super Bowls in as many trips with the New York Giants.
"Guys believe in Coach Parcells like you wouldn't believe," said New England safety Willie "Big Play" Clay. "He's been here and the man knows what he's talking about."
The once shaky Patriots defence suddenly seems to have jelled under Parcells and his defensive brain trust. In two post-season games, New England's no-name defence has executed to near perfection.
In fact, the Pats have not surrendered a post-season touchdown.

They held Pittsburgh to a mere three points in a divisional playoff game one week after the Steelers scored 42 against Indianapolis. And the high-powered Jacksonville offence produced just six points against New England in the AFC championship.
So while Green Bay is the stronger all around team, Parcells, given two weeks to prepare, just might find a way to beat them.
And if the Pats give Parcells his third championship, he will be the first coach in NFL history to win Super Bowls with two different teams.

Three titles would make Parcells the fourth coach to collect more than two Super crowns joining Chuck Noll of the Pittsburgh Steelers, Bill Walsh of the San Francisco 49ers and Joe Gibbs of the Washington Redskins.
"The guys that have done it more than twice, those guys are supermen," he said.
